summary: Muscongus Bay light in the St. George River approach: a 1855 brick tower after 1807 and 1830 towers, a 1925 rescue by its keeper, and a 1933 automation.

light.note: The archive gives 1805 as the year the station was established; LighthouseFriends gives 1807 as the year the light was first exhibited.

structures.note: Third tower on the island. The archive gives 45 ft (13.7 m) to the centre of the lantern.
First tower, built by contractors Benjamin Beal and Duncan W. Thaxter.
Second tower, built by Ezekiel D. Demuth.

access.note: Closed to the public during the seabird nesting season, 1 April to 31 August. Reached by boat; tower closed.

events.note: Station established (archive year; LighthouseFriends gives 1806 to 1807 for the first tower)
Massachusetts cedes the twelve-acre island to the United States; Beal and Thaxter build the wooden tower for $3,150
First exhibited with a fixed white light, focal plane 50 ft
Second tower of rubblestone built by Ezekiel D. Demuth

LighthouseFriends, describing the 1842 report: a gale destroyed the boatways 'the previous February', preventing use of the boat; Hanna's 1842 statement: a chimney blew down on '4th October last'. The statement gives no year for either; 1841 is inferred from the report date.
Inspector W. B. Franklin recommends rebuilding the towers on Franklin and Baker islands
Oil house built; cistern provided for the keeper's use
An ell added to the dwelling
Keeper A. J. Clinch is named in the fiscal 1917 saving-of-life table (page image checked, printed p. 54): the table gives the act as towing a disabled boat, with its occupant, to shore.
Keeper George E. Woodward gives food and a boat to fishermen marooned near the station (9 January 1925)
Converted to an automated acetylene apparatus and destaffed (archive: ca. 1933)
All structures except the tower and oil house burned
Island transferred to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
Coast Guard licenses Franklin Light Preservation Inc. to care for the lighthouse
Pier and helipad built with Coast Guard approval; state ordered them removed two years later

keepers.note: First keeper; the LighthouseFriends account says he stayed twenty-three years.

keepers.name: Thomas Hanna
keepers.note: Kept the light from 1830 until his son succeeded him in 1841 (LighthouseFriends quotes the son's 1842 statement).

keepers.name: James T. Hanna
keepers.note: Succeeded his father in 1841 and gave the 1842 keeper's statement quoted by LighthouseFriends.

keepers.name: George D. Pottle
keepers.note: Protected nesting terns on three islands near the station. Pottle estimated the colonies grew by about a thousand pairs in one season (the American Ornithologists' Union committee's 1901 report in The Auk, as LighthouseFriends quotes it).

keepers.name: Albert J. Clinch
keepers.note: Named in the Commissioner's fiscal 1917 saving-of-life table (printed p. 54, scan p. 265); the row was checked on the page image and gives the act as towing a disabled boat, with its occupant, to shore.

keepers.name: George E. Woodward
keepers.note: Went to the aid of marooned fishermen on 9 January 1925 (Lighthouse Service Bulletin, 1925).

wrecks.outcome: Marooned on an island near the station; keeper George E. Woodward gave them food and a boat

corrections.why: The brick tower standing on the island was built in 1855. The 1805 (and 1807) tower was a wooden tower by Beal and Thaxter, replaced in 1830 and again in 1855 (LighthouseFriends; archive year 1855).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The archive gives 1805 as the year the station was established. LighthouseFriends and the Rowlett directory give 1807 as the year the light was first exhibited, after Massachusetts ceded the island in 1806. The record keeps 1805 as the station year and the story gives both.
The wooden tower of 1807 and the rubblestone tower of 1830 were both replaced; the standing brick tower dates from 1855, as the archive and LighthouseFriends agree.

notes_for_editor: Sources disagree on the first year (archive 1805, LighthouseFriends 1807 first exhibition) and on distance (LighthouseFriends five miles from Friendship, the Fish and Wildlife Service six miles). LighthouseFriends gives the 1830 tower's builder and the 1842 keeper's statement, and quotes an 1842 report by I. W. P. Lewis and an 1853 inspector; those are cited as quoted by LighthouseFriends and no primary text was read. The Auk 1901 committee report is cited only as LighthouseFriends quotes it. The corpus lacks the 1842 and 1853 reports. Bulletin index entries for 'Chandler, Roscoe, keeper Franklin Island, assists power boat' (1918-1923 index, p. 284) were not verified in the bulletin text, so they are not used. The 1917 Commissioner entry (printed p. 54, scan p. 265) was checked on the page image: the row reads A. J. Clinch, keeper, Franklin Island Light Station, Me., with vessel 'Motor boat; William Collamore, owner' and act 'Towed disabled boat with occupant to shore'. The boat owner is a private person and is not named in the story. The fiscal 1917 table entry was matched by position in OCR and then confirmed on the page image. The Fish and Wildlife Service page was checked: it gives six miles and the 1 April to 31 August closure, but no 1973 transfer date, so the 1973 transfer rests on LighthouseFriends alone (footnote 4 removed from that sentence). LighthouseFriends gives the closure as ending 31 July in its history and 31 August in its visitor notes; the story states both. The 1842 gale and chimney events are LighthouseFriends' narration and Hanna's statement; neither gives a year, so the 1841 event year is inferred from the report date. LighthouseFriends is an all-rights-reserved site: facts and short quotations only. The 1998 and 2001-2003 pier events are LighthouseFriends' account; no other source read. Roster lines carry the archive's person slugs as printed by roster.py. The Coast Guard historian page was not reachable in its archived copy.
